Swiss Federal Supreme Court decision of June 22, 1988 (BGE 114 II 264) (translated with 
Deepl) 
1 of 10 
From the reasoning: 
1. In the appeal proceedings, the defendant challenges only the amount of the contractual 
penalty, which, contrary to the Commercial Court’s view, should be substantially reduced 
pursuant to Art. 163(3) OR. 
a) Under this provision, the judge must reduce an excessively high contractual penalty at his or 
her discretion. Restraint is called for here, if only because the penalty may, in principle, be set at 
any amount by the parties pursuant to Art. 163(1) OR and because contracts must be honored; the 
former stems from the fundamental principle of good faith in contracts, while the latter 
corresponds to the principle of freedom of contract. Judicial intervention in the contract is 
justified under these principles only if the agreed-upon amount is so high that it exceeds what is 
reasonable and still compatible with justice and equity (BGE 103 II 135 with references). The 
most important reason for such intervention lies in the fact that the statutory limits on freedom of 
contract under Art. 19/20 of the Swiss Code of Obligations (OR) relate to the circumstances at 
the time the contract was concluded, but the justification for the agreed penalty can only be 
properly assessed after a breach of contract has occurred (BGE 69 II 79; VON BÜREN, OR 
General Part, p. 411 et seq.). 
A reduction of the contractual penalty is justified in particular when there is a gross disproportion 
between the agreed amount and the claimant’s interest in enforcing it in full. The requirements 
for the justification and proportionality of the intervention are not determined in general terms 
but depend on the circumstances of the individual case (BGE 103 II 108 with references). These 
include, in particular, the nature and duration of the contract (BGE 38 II 102), the severity of the 
fault and the breach of contract (BGE 103 II 135, BGE 91 II 383), the claimant’s interest in 
compliance with the prohibition (BGE 103 II 135), and the economic situation of the parties 
involved (BGE 95 II 539 et seq.), particularly that of the obligated party 
(OSER/SCHÖNENBERGER, n. 16 on Art. 163 OR). Furthermore, any dependencies arising 
from the contractual relationship and the business experience of the parties must be taken into 
account. In the case of an employee—who is generally also the economically weaker party—a 
reduction is more justifiable than it would be between contractually equal and business-savvy 
parties (BECKER, n. 17 on Art. 163 CO; VON TUHR/ESCHER, CO General Part II, p. 285 et 
seq.).
